messages.subject: Expectation at mesh nodes
parts:
Hi,
Is there a way to get expectation of a spatial model such as g(intercept + s), where g is inverse link function and s is spatial "random effect" at the mesh nodes? What I want to do is to feed the expectations for inla.mesh.project and find volume under the estimated spatial surface.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Expectation at mesh nodes
parts:
On 19/03/14 08:43, Jussi wrote:
> Is there a way to get expectation of a spatial model such as g(intercept
> + s), where g is inverse link function and s is spatial "random effect"
> at the mesh nodes? What I want to do is to feed the expectations for
> inla.mesh.project and find volume under the estimated spatial surface.

You seem to be asking for two different things, so let's clear things
up: Let u(x) be the intercept+spatial effect at location x.

The (submitted) tutorial text available at
http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/papers/jss/lindgren.pdf
shows how to get the posteriors for intercept + spde model
into fitted.values in the output at arbitrary locations (just use
mesh$loc as coordinates to get the values at mesh nodes).
For small meshes an alternative is to use the "lincomb" feature instead.

Section 3.3 shows how to specify whether to apply a link function or
not. See also the r-inla.org FAQ entry about how to make predictions.

E(u(x)) is straightforward; no link specification needed, as any NA data
will not have a link function applied unless you specifically tell it to
do that. fitted.values will contain the posterior distributions
for u(x) at the mesh nodes.

E(g(u(x))) is the same as E(u(x)) except that you need to tell it to
actually apply the link function to in the prediction. fitted.values
will contain the posteriors for g(u(x)) at the mesh nodes.

Your final sentence seems to ask for

\int E( g(u(x)) ) dx

which is also easy once you have the gux=E(g(u(x))) result; simply evaluate
sum(gux * (inla.mesh.fem(mesh, order=1)$c1 %*% gux))
to get a simple integral approximation.

In order to get a better approximation you may want to do the
predictions of g(x(u)) on a slightly finer mesh than your model; this
is also straightforward: use fine.mesh$loc and
inla.mesh.fem(fine.mesh,...) above. fitted.values will contain the
posteriors for g(u(x)) at the nodes of the fine mesh.
But the model itself will still be piecewise linear for x(s).

Finn L
